primitives.name: Maximin Action Identification
primitives.verbatim_quote: It consists in identifying the best action in a game, when the player may sample random outcomes of sequentially chosen pairs of actions.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'i, j': 'action indices for players A and B respectively', 'μ_{i,j}': 'probability of player A winning given actions i and j', 'i*': 'optimal maximin action index'}
primitives.assumptions: Two-player zero-sum game with full information; actions are sampled sequentially; payoff probabilities are stationary.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When sampled outcomes fail to distinguish between top actions due to insufficient exploration or adversarial noise.

layer2.mapping: The maximin problem is isomorphic to best-arm identification in a strategic bandit model where arms represent action pairs and rewards correspond to win probabilities.
layer2.telemetry: Empirical probability of correctly identifying the ǫ-maximin action within confidence δ.

primitives.name: Maximin-LUCB Strategy
primitives.verbatim_quote: We propose two strategies for the fixed-confidence setting: Maximin-LUCB, based on lower- and upper- confidence bounds; and Maximin-Racing, which operates by successively eliminating the sub-optimal actions.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'L_t(i)': 'lower confidence bound for action i at time t', 'U_t(i)': 'upper confidence bound for action i at time t', 'τ': 'stopping time for recommendation'}
primitives.assumptions: Fixed-confidence setting; bounded reward distributions; sequential sampling of action pairs.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Failure occurs when confidence intervals do not sufficiently separate the best and worst actions, leading to incorrect elimination.

layer2.mapping: M-LUCB derives its kernel from UCB-style confidence bounds applied to the minimax payoff estimates across action pairs.
layer2.telemetry: Sample complexity and empirical error rate in identifying ǫ-maximin actions.

primitives.name: Maximin-Racing Strategy
primitives.verbatim_quote: We propose two strategies for the fixed-confidence setting: Maximin-LUCB, based on lower- and upper- confidence bounds; and Maximin-Racing, which operates by successively eliminating the sub-optimal actions.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'E_t': 'set of remaining candidate actions at time t', 't': 'round number', 'R_t': 'racing score difference threshold'}
primitives.assumptions: Sequential elimination of suboptimal actions; fixed-confidence constraint; bounded variance in sampled outcomes.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Failure when early eliminations incorrectly remove the true maximin action due to noisy estimates.

layer2.mapping: Maximin-Racing uses a racing mechanism to iteratively eliminate actions whose estimated minimax payoffs fall below a threshold, reducing sample complexity.
layer2.telemetry: Number of rounds until convergence and proportion of correct eliminations.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that in strategic games, identifying the best move requires balancing exploration of uncertain outcomes against exploitation of known advantages. The proposed framework models this as a two-stage process: first, sampling random outcomes of action pairs to estimate payoff distributions; second, applying confidence-based or elimination strategies to converge on the maximin action. This dualism mirrors classical multi-armed bandit paradigms but introduces strategic dependencies through the two-player interaction. The M-LUCB approach leverages lower and upper bounds on expected payoffs to guide sampling, ensuring that the final recommendation satisfies a fixed-confidence guarantee. Meanwhile, Maximin-Racing dynamically eliminates suboptimal actions based on score thresholds, trading off computational efficiency for potentially tighter bounds. Both methods rely on stochastic modeling of game states and assume that the underlying payoff structure admits a finite representation. Failure modes arise when the sampling process fails to distinguish between top candidates or when the game's inherent randomness masks the true value of actions. The theoretical grounding lies in best-arm identification literature, extended to strategic settings where actions are interdependent rather than independent.
